spots.name: Ubud Monkey Forest
spots.label: Monkey Forest

text.access_note: The street outside is open to anyone, but entry to the sanctuary is paid and parts of it, including the sacred temple areas, are closed to visitors, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: There are no railway or tram stops here, so head into Ubud and make your way to Jalan Monkey Forest, then go to the southern end of the street near the main entrance. Look for the stone entrance sign. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: In Padangtegal, in the Ubud area of Bali.
text.description:
Ubud Monkey Forest is a village-owned sanctuary in Padangtegal, Ubud, where tall trees, mossy stonework and a large troop of Balinese long-tailed macaques share the same few hectares. It covers about 10 hectares and has at least 115 tree species. As of 2023 about 1,260 macaques lived here. Three Hindu temples stand inside, all thought to date from around 1350. The place is still part of local spiritual life, so some areas are closed to visitors. That mix of jungle, old carved stone and animal life is why it photographs so well, and why a gentle, unhurried approach gets the best pictures.

Frame the stone entrance sign with the street's cafés and galleries around it, so the picture says where you are before you go in. Inside, two other spots are worth a frame. The stone bridge with dragon-headed railings over the ravine looks good with jungle and mossy statues at either end. The carved gateway of Pura Dalem Agung Padangtegal sits among the trees, and you shoot it from just outside, as the inner courtyard is for worshippers.

The macaques have lost their fear of people and may grab bags or climb on visitors. Keep your distance, avoid eye contact and never offer food. Let your zoom do the work rather than stepping closer.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the entrance sign and the street. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole entrance and the shopfronts. Inside, use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for monkeys and carved details, so you never need to get close.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the stone sign off-centre, leaving the street and shopfronts as context. If you want something different, the dragon-headed stone bridge over the ravine works well framed by jungle. The temple gateway of Pura Dalem Agung Padangtegal is best shot from just outside the gate, with the trees around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jalan Monkey Forest (near the main entrance at the southern end of the street). The stone sign at the sanctuary entrance with the street's cafés and galleries nearby, giving a sense of place before going inside. From here the sanctuary lies to the south-west. The photo shows the stone sign at the sanctuary entrance with the street's cafés and galleries nearby, giving a sense of place before you go inside.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the sign or the monkey's face, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright patches between the trees don't wash out. For moving monkeys, hold the shutter for a burst or use Live Photos and pick the best frame. Portrait mode works for a monkey sitting still, but only from a safe distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The street outside is a quieter option than the forest itself.

spots.alt: Ubud Monkey Forest, Ubud: a village-owned sanctuary in Padangtegal. Photo spot

text.access_note: The palace front can be seen from the street, but some areas inside may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
text.directions_text: Head for the centre of Ubud and ask your taxi or hired scooter to stop on Jalan Raya Ubud by the palace. Look for the carved walls and tall gates. Cross to the pavement directly opposite the front. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Ubud, on the main road, Jalan Raya Ubud. The palace is the large royal compound on this stretch, with its private family temple, Pura Marajan Agung, to the north.
text.description: Ubud Palace, officially Puri Saren Agung, was the official residence of Ubud's royal family, and the enclosure in front is also a residence for the royal family. It sits right on the main road in the town centre, and the palace front can be seen from the street. The picture is the front of the palace: carved walls, tall gates and detailed stonework, all in traditional Balinese style. The present palace dates from the reign of Tjokorda Putu Kandel (1800–1823). It was badly damaged in the 1917 earthquake, quickly restored, and opened to foreign guests in 1928. Many of the stone carvings are the work of the local artist I Gusti Nyoman Lempad. The palace is also known for its traditional dance shows, and the main pavilion usually hosts them at night. From the pavement opposite you can fit the whole frontage in one shot, then step closer for the detail. Look for the symmetry of the gates and the texture of the carved stone. Keep your phone steady and keep an eye on passing traffic and other visitors. Some areas inside may be ticketed, and photography can be restricted in sacred areas and during live performances, so check the official site before you go.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the palace front as you see it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you cannot fit the full gates and walls in. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the carvings and gate details.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the gate with the centre of the frame so the symmetry looks tidy. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. Include some of the carved wall at the edges to show the scale. For a different view, the Candi Bentar split gateway and the wooden Kul-Kul drum tower are both worth a look if you can reach them.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jalan Raya Ubud (on the pavement directly across from the palace front, framing the carved walls and towering gates). The palace front with its ornately carved walls and tall gates, seen from the street. On the pavement directly across from the palace front.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the carved stonework to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring down bright sky so the carvings stay detailed. Take a few frames in case people walk through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is a good bet for softer light and fewer people on the pavement. If you stay for the evening dance, remember that photography can be restricted during live performances, so ask first.

spots.name: Goa Gajah
spots.label: Goa Gajah

text.access_note: This is a ticketed temple complex and a place of worship, where visitors in shorts are given a sarong; check the official site before you go for entry details and opening times.
text.directions_text: From central Ubud, head south-east towards Bedulu village, about 5 km away. Look for signs to Goa Gajah, the Elephant Cave. From the entrance, walk down the stairs into the complex to reach the cave and the bathing pools. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: Goa Gajah is in Bedulu village, in Gianyar, on the south-eastern edge of the Ubud area, about 5 km from central Ubud. The site lies down a flight of stairs from the village entrance.
text.description:
Goa Gajah, the Elephant Cave, is a carved stone sanctuary set in a green hollow near Bedulu village. The cave mouth is framed by a crowded carving of a menacing face, thought to ward off evil spirits. The site is generally dated to the 9th to 11th centuries, and it mixes Hindu and Buddhist imagery. The cave was rediscovered by Dutch archaeologists in 1923, but the bathing pools were not uncovered until 1954.

The bathing pools make the best phone photo. Seven women statues hold water pitchers there, representing seven holy rivers, though one statue was lost in an earthquake. Stone spouts and figures sit in a tidy symmetrical row, with garden behind. A step or two higher than the pool level, both rows of spouts fit into one frame, and the repeating shapes suit a straight-on, centred shot.

The entrance to the cave is reached only by walking down a long flight of stairs, so wear comfortable shoes. The pools are the busiest corner, so arriving early gives you a cleaner frame. This is a working sacred place, so ask before photographing worshippers, don't block the doorway for long poses, and keep the flash off around people praying. If you also want the full demon face over the doorway, take that shot as well, and the older ruins and water in the valley below make a quieter third picture.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the row of spouts and statues over the bathing pools. If the pools feel too tight to fit in one frame, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x). Use telephoto (2x or more) for details, such as a single carved figure or the demon face over the cave doorway.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre yourself on the middle of the pools and turn on gridlines so both rows of spouts sit evenly either side. Keep the phone level so the symmetry reads clearly. For a second picture, walk to the cave doorway and frame the full carved demon face so the whole entrance fills the screen. The older ruins and water in the valley below the main site, at Tukad Pangkung, are another option.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the symmetrical-spouts shot, walk from there to the steps above the bathing pools. From this higher angle the row of stone spouts and statues over the pools fits in one photo, with the green garden behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone spouts to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if bright patches wash out the stone. Keep the flash off, because people may be praying nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is quieter, with fewer large groups at the pools than around midday.

spots.alt: Goa Gajah, Ubud: a carved stone sanctuary set in a green hollow near Bedulu village. Photo spot
